Talking World Atlas

Explore the world with your finger, like a tactile school atlas that talks. Slide over the map to hear oceans, continents, countries, cities, mountains, rivers, landmarks and famous walking trails. Zoom in to hear more detail. Everything works offline once the page has loaded.

      How to use

      Exploring with your finger

      Slide one finger over the map. It says what is underneath: at World zoom you hear oceans and continents; zoom in to hear countries and seas, then capitals, cities, mountains, rivers, lakes, landmarks, historic sites and walking trails.

      Sounds help you feel the shapes. A low warm note means you have crossed onto land, a soft watery whoosh means you have gone out to sea, a small tick means you have crossed a border, a bright chime means a place is under your finger, and a bubbling sound means a river. Sounds move left and right with your finger, and notes are a little higher in the north and lower in the south.

      Double-tap the map with one finger, without VoiceOver, to hear more about what is under your finger.

      With VoiceOver on

      VoiceOver normally takes over your touches, so the map has three ways in.

      One: pass-through. Touch the map, then double-tap and hold with one finger. When you hear a short tone, keep your finger down and slide it around. The atlas speaks as you move. Lift your finger to stop, and repeat to explore again.

      Two: Direct Touch. If your iPhone offers Direct Touch for Safari in the VoiceOver rotor or VoiceOver settings, turn it on while you are on the map, then slide your finger freely. Two fingers pinching apart zoom in and pinching together zoom out. Turn Direct Touch off again to use the buttons.

      Three: the buttons. Move north, south, east and west move a cursor across the map, a step at a time, and say what is there. Zoom in and Zoom out change the detail. What's here gives a full description of the cursor's position, More about this reads the information for the place, and What's nearby lists the closest places with distance and direction.

      You can also turn VoiceOver off with the accessibility shortcut, triple-clicking the side button, and choose the atlas's own voice in Settings. Then you can explore freely with one finger and pinch to zoom. Triple-click again to bring VoiceOver back.

      Searching

      Type a place in the search box and choose Find. The atlas moves the map there at a suitable zoom, reads its information, and lists other matches. Small spelling mistakes are fine. Then explore outward from there with your finger or the move buttons.

      Zoom levels

      Level 1, World: oceans and continents. Level 2, Continent: countries, seas, great capitals and natural wonders. Level 3, Country: capitals, big cities, major rivers, lakes, mountains and famous sites. Level 4, Region: more cities, mountains, rivers and trails. Level 5, Local: towns, landmarks and historic sites. Level 6, Close-up: landmarks inside a city. Zooming in centres the map on your cursor.

      Keyboard

      On the map: arrow keys move the cursor, plus and minus zoom, Enter says what's here, Space reads more about this, and N lists nearby places.

      Good to know

      Borders and coastlines are simplified, so near a coast or border the atlas can be a few miles out. Disputed borders are shown as Natural Earth draws them, which is not a judgement on any dispute. This is a learning atlas, not a navigation aid.

      Sources and credits

      Map data: Natural Earth (naturalearthdata.com), which is in the public domain. Used: Admin 0 countries at 1:50 million, marine areas at 1:10 million, rivers and lake centrelines, lakes and physical regions at 1:50 million, populated places and elevation and geographic points at 1:10 million. Shapes were simplified with mapshaper.

      Country populations are Natural Earth's estimates, mostly for 2019. Areas are calculated from the simplified shapes and are approximate. Land neighbours are worked out from shared borders in the map data.

      Descriptions of countries, cities, landmarks, historic sites, natural wonders, mountains, rivers, lakes and trails were written for this atlas from general reference knowledge. Heights and lengths are rounded.

      Sounds are made live by the app; there are no recordings. Made for Ahsan, November 2026.
